name: Gibbons-Maeda-Garfinkle-Horowitz-Strominger Dilaton Black Hole
description: The static, spherically symmetric charged black hole of low energy string theory, a solution of Einstein's equations with a Maxwell field and a scalar field, the dilaton, coupled to it. On the plane of time and radius its metric is Schwarzschild's, with one horizon at the Schwarzschild radius for every charge and no inner horizon, and the area of its spheres vanishes at the singularity.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ explicit, and $r_s$ and $r_d$ are lengths. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: Gary Gibbons found black holes carrying scalar, electric, and magnetic charges among the solutions of $N = 4$ supergravity in 1982 [gibbons1982dilaton]. In a limiting case they have zero temperature, and Gibbons exhibited solutions with several such holes in static equilibrium [gibbons1982dilaton]. With Kei-ichi Maeda he took them up again in 1988, in theories of any dimension that couple gravity to Maxwell fields and antisymmetric tensor fields through a dilaton [gibbons1988]. The properties of their solutions depend on the coupling constant of the dilaton, and a critical value of it separates two kinds of behaviour of the temperature of a charged black hole in the extreme limit [gibbons1988].¶David Garfinkle, Gary Horowitz, and Andrew Strominger found the solution independently in 1991, in a simpler form, as the static, spherically symmetric charged black hole of low energy string theory [garfinkle1991, horowitz1992]. Their solutions are labelled by the mass $M$, the charge $Q$, and the value of the dilaton at infinity [garfinkle1991]. With that value set to zero, and in units with $G = c = 1$, the Einstein metric is $ds^2 = -(1 - 2M/r)dt^2 + dr^2/(1 - 2M/r) + r(r - Q^2/M)d\Omega^2$ [horowitz1992]. On the plane of $t$ and $r$ it is Schwarzschild's metric, with the horizon at $r = 2M$ for every charge, and the area of the spheres vanishes at $r = Q^2/M$, a curvature singularity [horowitz1992]. The black hole has no inner horizon, and for $Q^2 < 2M^2$ its Penrose diagram is Schwarzschild's [horowitz1992]. Its dilaton charge is $D = Q^2/2M$, fixed by the mass and the charge in agreement with the no hair theorems [horowitz1992].¶At the largest charge, $Q^2 = 2M^2$, the singularity coincides with the horizon, whose area is zero [horowitz1992]. Strings move in the string metric, the Einstein metric multiplied by $e^{2\varphi}$ for the dilaton $\varphi$ [horowitz1992]. An electrically charged hole and the magnetically charged hole dual to it share one Einstein metric, and the dilaton of one is minus the dilaton of the other, so their string metrics differ [horowitz1992]. For the magnetically charged hole at $Q^2 = 2M^2$ the string metric is $ds^2 = -dt^2 + (1 - 2M/r)^{-2}dr^2 + r^2d\Omega^2$, which for $r > 2M$ is geodesically complete and has no curvature singularity [garfinkle1991, horowitz1992]. A surface of constant $t$ there is that of the extreme Reissner-Nordström black hole, an infinitely long throat, and the dilaton is linear in the proper distance along it [horowitz1992]. Steven Giddings and Strominger showed in 1992 that near the extremal limit a neighbourhood of the horizon is closely approximated by the product of a two dimensional black hole with a sphere, so that a two dimensional field theory describes the scattering of particles of long wavelength off the hole [giddings1992].¶The Hawking temperature depends only on the metric of the plane of $t$ and $r$, so it is Schwarzschild's, $T = 1/8\pi M$, for every charge up to $Q^2 = 2M^2$ [horowitz1992]. John Preskill, Patricia Schwarz, Alfred Shapere, Sandip Trivedi, and Frank Wilczek argued in 1991 that the description of a black hole as a thermal object breaks down as the extreme limit is approached [preskill1991]. Christoph Holzhey and Wilczek analysed the perturbations around the extreme holes in 1992 and found the holes protected by mass gaps or potential barriers, which remove them from thermal contact with the world outside [holzhey1992]. They described the extreme dilaton black holes as "doing their best to behave like normal elementary particles" [holzhey1992]. Renata Kallosh, Andrei Linde, Tomás Ortín, Amanda Peet, and Antoine Van Proeyen showed the same year that the extreme holes saturate the supersymmetry bound of $N = 4$ supergravity, $M \ge (|Q| + |P|)/\sqrt{2}$ for an electric charge $Q$ and a magnetic charge $P$, which is also the condition that no singularity is naked [kallosh1992].¶Ashoke Sen constructed the rotating charged black hole of heterotic string theory in 1992, a solution carrying mass, charge, and angular momentum [sen1992]. James Horne and Horowitz showed the same year that an arbitrarily small angular momentum changes the properties of the extremal charged dilaton black hole qualitatively [horne1992]. Horne and Horowitz gave the dilaton a mass in 1993, and found that black holes large compared with its Compton wavelength resemble the Reissner-Nordström solution while smaller ones resemble the black holes of the massless dilaton [horne1993]. Ruth Gregory and Jeffrey Harvey argued in 1993 that a hole of charge $Q$ coupled to a dilaton of mass $m$ has a single horizon when $Qm$ is below order one [gregory1993]. Fay Dowker, Jerome Gauntlett, David Kastor, and Jennie Traschen generalised the C-metric in 1994 to a pair of oppositely charged dilaton black holes in uniform acceleration, and Ernst's metric to the same pair in a magnetic field [dowker1994].¶Eric Hirschmann, Luis Lehner, Steven Liebling, and Carlos Palenzuela evolved single black holes and merging pairs of them in Einstein-Maxwell-dilaton theory in 2018, and concluded that for the small charges they considered such systems are difficult to distinguish from their counterparts in general relativity [hirschmann2018]. Yosuke Mizuno and eight coauthors simulated a magnetised accretion flow onto a Kerr black hole and onto a dilaton black hole that year, computed the image of each as the Event Horizon Telescope would record it, and found the two extremely difficult to tell apart with the telescope's array of 2017 [mizuno2018]. Prashant Kocherlakota, Luciano Rezzolla, and the Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration used the size of the shadow of M87* in 2021 to constrain the charges of a variety of black holes, and found the measurements "already sufficient to rule out that M87* is a highly charged dilaton black hole" [kocherlakota2021].

related.text: The black hole with no charge, $r_d = 0$. With charge, the plane of $t$ and $r$ keeps Schwarzschild's metric and the spheres shrink [horowitz1992].
The charged black hole of Einstein-Maxwell theory, with no dilaton. It has an inner horizon, and the dilaton black hole has none [horowitz1992].

The extreme magnetic black hole of the same family with the dilaton coupled at strength $\sqrt{3}$, Kaluza and Klein's value. Lifted to five dimensions its singularity goes away and it is a smooth vacuum solution [duff1994].
The charged, rotating black hole of Einstein-Maxwell theory. Ashoke Sen built its counterpart in heterotic string theory in 1992, a black hole with mass, charge, and angular momentum [sen1992].

Two black holes accelerating apart. Dowker, Gauntlett, Kastor, and Traschen generalised it in 1994 to a pair of oppositely charged dilaton black holes, and used it to describe their creation in a magnetic field [dowker1994].
In the limit of the extremal magnetic charge, the region around the horizon is closely approximated by Witten's black hole in two dimensions times a sphere [giddings1992].

coordinates.name: Static Spherical

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$ for a hole of mass $M$

Radius at which the area of the spheres of the Einstein metric vanishes, $r_d = 2r_q^2/r_s$ with $r_q^2 = Q^2G/(4\pi\epsilon_0c^4)$ the square of the charge radius, which is $Q^2/M$ in units with $G = c = 1$; $0 \le r_d \le r_s$, and $r_d = r_s$ is the extremal charge $Q^2 = 2M^2$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time, and take components of the Einstein metric in the chart $x^0 = ct$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
geodesics: \ddot{r} + \dfrac{r_s\left(r - r_s\right)}{2r^3}\dot{t}^2 - \dfrac{r_s}{2r\left(r - r_s\right)}\dot{r}^2 - \dfrac{\left(r - r_s\right)\left(2r - r_d\right)}{2r}\dot{\theta}^2 - \dfrac{\left(r - r_s\right)\left(2r - r_d\right)\sin^2\theta}{2r}\dot{\phi}^2 = 0

coordinates.name: Outgoing Eddington-Finkelstein

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$ for a hole of mass $M$

Radius at which the area of the spheres of the Einstein metric vanishes, $r_d = 2r_q^2/r_s$ with $r_q^2 = Q^2G/(4\pi\epsilon_0c^4)$ the square of the charge radius, which is $Q^2/M$ in units with $G = c = 1$; $0 \le r_d \le r_s$, and $r_d = r_s$ is the extremal charge $Q^2 = 2M^2$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(u, r, \theta, \phi)$ on the Einstein metric, with the retarded time $u = ct - r_*$ a length, where $r_* = r + r_s\ln\left|r/r_s - 1\right|$.

coordinates.name: Ingoing Eddington-Finkelstein

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$ for a hole of mass $M$

Radius at which the area of the spheres of the Einstein metric vanishes, $r_d = 2r_q^2/r_s$ with $r_q^2 = Q^2G/(4\pi\epsilon_0c^4)$ the square of the charge radius, which is $Q^2/M$ in units with $G = c = 1$; $0 \le r_d \le r_s$, and $r_d = r_s$ is the extremal charge $Q^2 = 2M^2$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(v, r, \theta, \phi)$ on the Einstein metric, with the advanced time $v = ct + r_*$ a length, where $r_* = r + r_s\ln\left|r/r_s - 1\right|$.

coordinates.name: String Metric, Magnetic Charge

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$ for a hole of mass $M$

Radius at which the area of the spheres of the Einstein metric vanishes, $r_d = 2r_q^2/r_s$ with $r_q^2 = Q^2G/(4\pi\epsilon_0c^4)$ the square of the charge radius, which is $Q^2/M$ in units with $G = c = 1$; $0 \le r_d \le r_s$, and $r_d = r_s$ is the extremal charge $Q^2 = 2M^2$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ the areal radius, and take components of the string metric $e^{2\varphi}g_{\mu\nu}$ of the magnetically charged hole, with $g_{\mu\nu}$ the Einstein metric and $e^{-2\varphi} = 1 - r_d/r$, in the chart $x^0 = ct$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
geodesics: \ddot{r} - \dfrac{\left(r - r_s\right)\left(r_d - r_s\right)}{2r^2\left(r - r_d\right)}\dot{t}^2 - \dfrac{r\,r_d + r\,r_s - 2r_s\,r_d}{2r\left(r - r_d\right)\left(r - r_s\right)}\dot{r}^2 - \dfrac{\left(r - r_d\right)\left(r - r_s\right)}{r}\dot{\theta}^2 - \dfrac{\left(r - r_d\right)\left(r - r_s\right)\sin^2\theta}{r}\dot{\phi}^2 = 0

coordinates.name: String Metric, Electric Charge

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$ for a hole of mass $M$

Radius at which the area of the spheres of the Einstein metric vanishes, $r_d = 2r_q^2/r_s$ with $r_q^2 = Q^2G/(4\pi\epsilon_0c^4)$ the square of the charge radius, which is $Q^2/M$ in units with $G = c = 1$; $0 \le r_d \le r_s$, and $r_d = r_s$ is the extremal charge $Q^2 = 2M^2$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time, and take components of the string metric $e^{2\varphi}g_{\mu\nu}$ of the electrically charged hole, with $g_{\mu\nu}$ the Einstein metric and $e^{2\varphi} = 1 - r_d/r$, in the chart $x^0 = ct$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
geodesics: \ddot{r} + \dfrac{\left(r - r_s\right)\left(r\,r_d + r\,r_s - 2r_s\,r_d\right)}{2r^3\left(r - r_d\right)}\dot{t}^2 + \dfrac{r_d - r_s}{2\left(r - r_d\right)\left(r - r_s\right)}\dot{r}^2 - \left(r - r_s\right)\dot{\theta}^2 - \left(r - r_s\right)\sin^2\theta\,\dot{\phi}^2 = 0
